title: Was the Woman Rescued from a Berlin Canal Really Anastasia?
description:
In 1920, a woman who refused to give her name was rescued beside a Berlin canal. She later became linked to Princess Anastasia. A court case, two preserved samples, and two graves in a Russian forest each led the question of her identity toward a different answer.

This episode follows the events and the discovery of evidence in order. It separates what the German court actually ruled from comparisons of Anderson's samples with the empress's and Maucher's maternal lines, and from the conclusions of two 2009 studies about the five children and the specific identity of the girl in the second grave.

We tell the story with original, sourced diagrams, comparisons, and evidence cards. Three historical photographs are labeled with verifiable dates and collections. The diagrams are modern editorial illustrations, not images of the scene, the original ruling, actual samples, or human remains; we do not reconstruct Anna Anderson's face. The account of the 1970 ruling was checked against a scan of the court document preserved by a third party. The full text of the 1995 Nature Genetics paper is paywalled, so our account of the samples relies only on accessible bibliographic records, a researcher interview, and institutional explanations. The maternal-line and grave cards are modern teaching diagrams, not test records or photographs of remains. Narration is in Traditional Chinese; English, Japanese, and Korean titles, descriptions, and optional CC captions are also available. Information current as of 2026-10-14.

j6u5.text: In February 1920, a woman was rescued beside a Berlin canal.

v201.text: She gave no name, and police could not establish her identity.

dszz.text: Two years later, someone at the hospital linked her to Anastasia.

v202.text: But the case file offers two accounts of who said it first.

ykiq.text: In 1970, the Federal Court of Justice was to review an earlier ruling.

pfpa.text: Yet another woman's name appeared in the case file.

dw29.text: After her death, preserved tissue and hair reached a laboratory.

v203.text: Could those two samples tell us who she was?

pxbi.text: In 2007, someone noticed fragments on the ground in a Russian forest.

v204.text: Among the tiny pieces, researchers hoped to find two children.

cr5q.text: Was that unnamed woman in Berlin really Anastasia?

c63r.text: People later called her Anna Anderson; then, she refused to discuss her family.

uq5m.text: People guessed at her past from her words and appearance.

cap5.text: Those guesses met a gap left by the Russian royal family.

qwh4.text: Nicholas II and family were killed in 1918.

4jhc.text: But rumors still surrounded what had happened to the children.

n3d8.text: If she was the princess, those two events had to fit together.

9tfu.text: Who first brought Anastasia's name into the hospital room?

uqyb.text: In 1922, visitors began testing her with memories of royal life.

u6iw.text: This photo shows the royal Anastasia, not the woman in the hospital.

hcra.text: Then the hospital's speculation spread beyond its walls.

kvce.text: One account says she first claimed to be the princess.

jnga.text: Another says someone else named her first.

smmb.text: The ruling never settles who spoke first, as we asked at the start.

x2py.text: If the first claim is unclear, how do we identify her?

egvx.text: In 1928, a distant royal relative invited her to America.

28mj.text: How to identify her? Relatives could testify, but hosting her proved nothing.

2scy.text: Witnesses close to the royals said she was not the princess.

8nrj.text: Eventually, all these statements reached the court.

kv2b.text: An inheritance case turned speculation into a question of evidence.

kyrc.text: What would she need to prove to have her claim recognized in court?

26m8.text: The court required verifiable identity evidence to support her claim.

2ap4.text: It was hearing a civil claim, not a criminal fraud case.

fba5.text: Anderson sought payment and recognition of inheritance rights.

v209.text: She asked the court to confirm an earlier inheritance certificate was wrong.

v210.text: Without proof she was the princess, those property claims lost their basis.

xhf4.text: They offered another identity claim and testimony.

sywj.text: Remember the name in the file? Missing factory worker Franziska Schanzkowska.

euyy.text: The judges had to weigh how her relatives identified her.

sexv.text: In 1967, the lower court finally delivered its ruling.

v212.text: It compared, point by point, whom witnesses had seen years before.

95fq.text: Would the court accept her claim to be the princess?

wmiq.text: The lower court found she had not proved she was the princess.

qyt5.text: Anderson appealed on points of law; the court reviewed law and procedure.

i2rk.text: In 1970, the Federal Court of Justice dismissed her appeal on points of law.

y57g.text: The ruling from our opening left her princess identity unproved.

8erd.text: It left the factory worker claim outside its ruling.

v227.text: Later, her samples would add another layer of evidence to that lead.

bnbr.text: The court did not judge her motive; the royal family's grave was missing.

4uuj.text: A lead emerged only in the late 1970s: geologist Avdonin found the first grave.

et4h.text: He and several friends kept its location secret for years.

yqep.text: The grave was formally excavated in 1991.

v215.text: It held nine sets of remains; four belonged to attendants.

2pva.text: Researchers identified Nicholas II, his wife, and three daughters.

s4mq.text: But of the five children, a boy and a girl were still missing.

73wj.text: That gap alone could not settle Anderson's identity.

bxmt.text: In 1995, samples she left behind entered a research report.

v216.text: The tissue came from a pathology slide preserved by a hospital.

v217.text: Hair kept in an envelope became the second sample for testing.

bp4e.text: Remember the opening samples? Researchers compared their maternal sequences.

xx8w.text: This genetic feature passes down the maternal line.

4yw7.text: First, Anderson's two samples matched each other.

v218.text: At first, neither team knew about the other; they shared results afterward.

8hyx.text: But did her maternal line match the empress's?

ix4m.text: If her mother was the empress, mtDNA should match.

fa8j.text: But neither sample matched the empress's known maternal reference.

jmhr.text: They found another maternal reference, too.

pgcg.text: Its donor, Carl Maucher, was a maternal relative of Schanzkowska.

v223.text: Anderson's maternal DNA matched Maucher's sample.

v225.text: But maternal relatives can share that sequence too.

v226.text: Back to those samples: a maternal clue, but no other real name from them alone.

xz9y.text: The first grave's two gaps needed other evidence.

dm7x.text: After the first grave, several searches for another nearby came up empty.

v2jq.text: Remember the fragments in the forest? They came from a second grave.

v219.text: Amateur archaeologists found fragments; officials investigated.

j43h.text: The sites lay about 70 meters apart.

v220.text: The official team catalogued 44 bone and tooth fragments.

yv8b.text: However small, the fragments had to be linked to a family.

znfv.text: Researchers did not name the children by site alone.

g6ne.text: They compared both graves' samples with relatives' data.

7sxb.text: Maternal DNA traced their mother's line.

h9hy.text: The boy's paternal DNA provided a third comparison.

b5hx.text: All three results pointed to the same family.

jptu.text: The new grave from our opening held their son Alexei.

92k7.text: The other child was one of the royal couple's four daughters.

v228.text: Russian anthropologists thought grave one lacked Maria.

v229.text: US researchers thought Anastasia was; could the new sample distinguish them?

ce8r.text: In 2009, researchers examined that daughter's genetic results.

zwkk.text: But the genetic results could not distinguish Maria from Anastasia.

dkkf.text: That year, another team combined data from both graves.

ufh6.text: Together, the graves held all five children of Nicholas II and his wife.
